clinicalPearls: Avascular necrosis of the scaphoid in the absence of a preceding acute fracture
It presents with insidious radial-sided wrist pain and tenderness, worse with activity and loading
It is distinguished from scaphoid fracture nonunion, in which osteonecrosis follows a known fracture
Associations include corticosteroid use, chemotherapy and other causes of osteonecrosis, though many cases are idiopathic
MRI is the most sensitive investigation and shows loss of the scaphoid blood supply and marrow changes
Management ranges from immobilisation in early disease to surgical options for advanced collapse and arthritis
reference.pathophysiology: Preiser disease is osteonecrosis of the scaphoid arising without an antecedent fracture, attributed to compromise of its already precarious blood supply, which enters predominantly distally so that the proximal pole is vulnerable to ischaemia. Impaired perfusion causes bone death, and with continued loading the necrotic scaphoid can fragment and collapse, altering carpal mechanics and leading to degenerative wrist arthritis. Systemic risk factors for osteonecrosis contribute in some cases, while others remain idiopathic.
additionalInvestigations: MRI to detect osteonecrosis and assess viability
Radiographs for sclerosis, fragmentation and collapse
History for corticosteroid, chemotherapy or other osteonecrosis risk factors
CT to define bony collapse where surgery is considered
Exclusion of an occult prior fracture
redFlags: Rapid progression of pain and deformity
Features suggesting an alternative aggressive bone lesion
reference.prognosis: Outcomes vary; early disease may stabilise with conservative treatment or revascularisation, but progressive collapse leads to arthritis that may require salvage surgery.
pitfalls: Confusing it with scaphoid fracture nonunion
Missing the diagnosis on early radiographs before MRI changes
Delaying treatment until collapse and arthritis are established
management: No disease-specific drug therapy exists; early disease is managed conservatively with wrist immobilisation, activity modification and analgesia including NSAIDs
Joint-preserving surgery such as revascularisation with a vascularised bone graft for viable but ischaemic scaphoids in early disease
Salvage procedures such as proximal row carpectomy, partial wrist fusion or wrist denervation for scaphoid collapse and established arthritis
Address contributing osteonecrosis risk factors such as corticosteroid or chemotherapy exposure
Serial MRI to assess scaphoid vascularity, disease progression and treatment response
Referral to hand surgery for staging and surgical planning
